- Also methods: `refresh()`, `back()`, `forward()`

**5. useLinkStatus Hook** (NEW)
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/04-functions/use-link-status.md`
- Introduced in v15.3.0

- Must be used within descendant component of `<Link>`
- Shows pending state during navigation for slow networks
- Graceful handling with animation delay and initial opacity

**6. Linking and Navigating Guide**
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/01-getting-started/04-linking-and-navigating.md`
- **Core Navigation Concepts**:

### CACHING & CACHE COMPONENTS

**1. Cache Components (NEW MAJOR FEATURE)**
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/01-getting-started/08-caching.md`
- **Enable with**: `cacheComponents: true` in next.config.ts
- **`use cache` Directive**: Mark functions/components as cacheable
  - File-level: `'use cache'` at top caches all exports
  - Function-level: `'use cache'` in function body
  - Component-level: `'use cache'` in async component
- **Data-level caching**: Cache individual functions
- **UI-level caching**: Cache entire components/pages
- All with `use cache` must be async
- Works with Partial Prerendering (PPR) by default

**2. use cache Directive**
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/01-directives/use-cache.md`
- Comprehensive directive for caching at build and runtime
- **Cache Keys**: Built ID, Function ID, serializable arguments, HMR refresh hash
- **Serialization**: Must follow React Server Component serialization rules
- **Constraints**: Cannot access `cookies()`, `headers()`, `searchParams` directly (pass as args)
- **Runtime caching**: In-memory LRU for serverless; persists in self-hosted
- **Nested caching**: Outer cache uses its own lifetime if explicit `cacheLife`
- **Interleaving**: Pass compositional slots (`children`, Server Actions) through without caching them
- **Default profile**: 5 min stale, 15 min revalidate, never expires
- **Environment support**: Node.js server, Docker, Adapters (not static export)

**3. cacheLife Function**
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/04-functions/cacheLife.md`
- Configure cache lifetime for `use cache` functions
- **Preset Profiles**:
  - `'seconds'`: 30s stale, 1s revalidate, 1 min expire (real-time)
  - `'minutes'`: 5 min stale, 1 min revalidate, 1 hour expire (frequent updates)
  - `'hours'`: 5 min stale, 1 hour revalidate, 1 day expire (multiple daily updates)
  - `'days'`: 5 min stale, 1 day revalidate, 1 week expire (daily updates)
  - `'weeks'`: 5 min stale, 1 week revalidate, 30 days expire (weekly updates)
  - `'max'`: 5 min stale, 30 days revalidate, 1 year expire (rarely changes)
  - `'default'`: 5 min stale, 15 min revalidate, never expires
- **Custom profiles** in next.config.ts
- **Inline profiles** for one-off cases: `cacheLife({ stale: 300, revalidate: 900, expire: 3600 })`
- **Properties**:
  - `stale`: Client-side cache duration (minimum 30s)
  - `revalidate`: Background regeneration interval
  - `expire`: Maximum time before sync regeneration
- Short-lived caches (< 5 min) become dynamic holes excluded from prerender

**4. cacheTag Function**
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/04-functions/cacheTag.md`
- Tag cached entries for on-demand invalidation
- `cacheTag('tag-name')` or `cacheTag('tag1', 'tag2')`
- Max 256 chars per tag, max 128 tags
- Idempotent: applying same tag multiple times has no additional effect

**5. updateTag Function** (NEW)
- **File**: `/vercel/sandbox/node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/04-functions/updateTag.md`
- **Only in Server Actions** (not Route Handlers)

- `updateTag('tag-name')`
- Next request waits for fresh data (no stale content)
- Differs from `revalidateTag`: updateTag always waits, revalidateTag can stale-while-revalidate

- **Auto Prefetch**: Links in viewport, configurable per-route

1 --- 2 title: Designing view transitions 3 description: Learn how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation, loading, and content changes in a Next.js app. 4 nav_title: View transitions 5 --- 6 7 In web apps, route changes replace the entire page at once. One set of elements disappears, another appears, with no visual connection between them. A user selects a photo thumbnail to view it in detail on another page. They are the same image, but nothing on screen communicates that. 8 9 Apps that need these transitions typically rely on complex animation libraries that manage mount/unmount lifecycles, track element positions across routes, and coordinate timing manually, to animate how elements enter, exit, and move between states. 10 11 React's `` component integrates with the browser's [View Transitions API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API) to handle this declaratively. You name the elements that should persist, and the browser animates between their old and new positions. 12 13 This guide walks through four patterns that cover the most common cases: morphing shared elements, animating loading states, adding directional navigation, and crossfading content within the same route. 14 15 ## Example 16 17 As an example, we'll build a photography gallery called _Frames_. 18 19 We'll start by morphing a thumbnail into a hero image (shared elements), then animate the loading skeleton into real content (Suspense reveals), add directional slides for forward and back navigation (route transitions), and finish with crossfades for switching between photographer tabs (same-route transitions). 20 21 You can find the resources used in this example here: 22 23 - [Demo](https://react-view-transitions-demo.labs.vercel.dev) 24 - [Code](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo) 25 26 Before starting, enable view transitions in your Next.js config: 27 28 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 29 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 30 31 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 32 experimental: { 33 viewTransition: true, 34 }, 35 } 36 37 export default nextConfig 38 ``` 39 40 > [!NOTE] 41 > The View Transitions API is supported in all major browsers, though some animations may behave differently in Safari. Without browser support, your application works normally, the transitions simply do not animate. 42 43 Then import the `ViewTransition` component from React: 44 45 ```tsx 46 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 47 ``` 48 49 `` animations are activated by [Transitions](https://react.dev/reference/react/useTransition), [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense), and [`useDeferredValue`](https://react.dev/reference/react/useDeferredValue). Regular `setState` calls do not trigger them. In Next.js, route navigations are transitions, so `` animations activate automatically during navigation. 50 51 ### Step 1: Morph a thumbnail into a hero image 52 53 The gallery displays photos in a grid. Clicking a photo opens a detail page with a larger version of the same image. Without transitions, the thumbnail disappears and the hero appears. Nothing connects them visually. The user has to scan the detail page to confirm they clicked the right photo. 54 55 In motion design, when an object persists across a cut, it communicates continuity. The viewer understands they are looking at the same thing, not a replacement. This is the most important transition pattern: **shared element morphing**. 56 57 Wrap both the grid thumbnail and the detail hero in `` with the same `name`: 58 59 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 60 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 61 import Image from 'next/image' 62 import Link from 'next/link' 63 64 function PhotoGrid({ photos }) { 65 return ( 66
67 {photos.map((photo) => ( 68 69 70 71 72 73 ))} 74
75 ) 76 } 77 ``` 78 79 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/photo-content.tsx" 80 import { ViewTransition } from 'react' 81 import Image from 'next/image' 82 83 async function PhotoContent({ id }) { 84 const photo = await getPhoto(id) 85 86 return ( 87 88 89 90 ) 91 } 92 ``` 93 94 The `name` prop creates identity. React finds elements with the same name on the old and new pages, then animates between their size and position automatically. No additional props are needed for the morph to work. 95 96 If we click a thumbnail now, the image scales and repositions from its grid cell to the hero slot. Navigating back reverses the morph. The user sees one object moving, not two objects swapping. 97 98 #### Customizing the morph animation 99 100 To control the morph CSS, add `share="morph"`. This assigns the `morph` class to the view transition, which you can target with CSS pseudo-elements. For example, to soften the morph mid-flight with a [`blur`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/filter-function/blur) keyframe: 101 102 ```tsx 103 104 105 106 ``` 107 108 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 109 ::view-transition-group(.morph) { 110 animation-duration: 400ms; 111 } 112 ::view-transition-image-pair(.morph) { 113 animation-name: via-blur; 114 } 115 @keyframes via-blur { 116 30% { 117 filter: blur(3px); 118 } 119 } 120 ``` 121 122 The blur hides pixel-level interpolation artifacts during the transition. At 400ms, the morph is slow enough to register but fast enough to feel direct. 123 124 ### Step 2: Animate loading states with Suspense reveals 125 126 The photo detail page loads its content asynchronously. While data is in flight, a Suspense boundary shows a skeleton. When the data resolves, the skeleton is replaced by the real content. 127 128 Without a transition, the swap is instant. The skeleton vanishes and the content pops in. 129 130 In motion design, vertical direction encodes hierarchy. Content sliding up communicates arrival. Content sliding down communicates departure. The pair together creates a handoff: the placeholder yields to the real thing. 131 132 Wrap the Suspense fallback in a `ViewTransition` with an exit animation, and the content in a `ViewTransition` with an enter animation: 133 134 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 135 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 136 137 export default async function PhotoPage({ params }) { 138 const { id } = await params 139 140 return ( 141 144 145 146 } 147 > 148 149 150 151 152 ) 153 } 154 ``` 155 156 The `default="none"` prop prevents this `ViewTransition` from animating during unrelated transitions, like the shared element morph from Step 1. Without it, every transition on the page would trigger every `ViewTransition`'s animation. 157 158 The CSS animations use asymmetric timing. The exit is fast (150ms). The enter is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes: 159 160 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 161 :root { 162 --duration-exit: 150ms; 163 --duration-enter: 210ms; 164 } 165 166 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 167 animation: 168 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 169 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 170 } 171 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 172 animation: 173 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 174 400ms ease-in both slide-y; 175 } 176 177 @keyframes fade { 178 from { 179 filter: blur(3px); 180 opacity: 0; 181 } 182 to { 183 filter: blur(0); 184 opacity: 1; 185 } 186 } 187 @keyframes slide-y { 188 from { 189 transform: translateY(10px); 190 } 191 to { 192 transform: translateY(0); 193 } 194 } 195 ``` 196 197 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter animation means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it appears. 198 199 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 200 201 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 202 203 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 204 205 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 206 207 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 208 209 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 210 211 {/* photo thumbnail */} 212 213 ``` 214 215 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 216 217 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 218 219 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 220 221 ← Gallery 222 223 ``` 224 225 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 226 227 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 228 229 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 230 243 {/* page content */} 244 245 ``` 246 247 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (like initial page loads) produce no animation. 248 249 The CSS for directional slides: 250 251 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 252 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 253 --slide-offset: -60px; 254 animation: 255 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 256 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 257 } 258 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 259 --slide-offset: 60px; 260 animation: 261 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 262 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 263 } 264 265 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 266 --slide-offset: 60px; 267 animation: 268 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 269 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 270 } 271 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 272 --slide-offset: -60px; 273 animation: 274 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 275 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 276 } 277 278 @keyframes slide { 279 from { 280 translate: var(--slide-offset); 281 } 282 to { 283 translate: 0; 284 } 285 } 286 ``` 287 288 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 289 290 #### Anchoring the header 291 292 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 293 294 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 295 296 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 297
298 {/* navigation links */} 299
300 ``` 301 302 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 303 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 304 animation: none; 305 z-index: 100; 306 } 307 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 308 display: none; 309 } 310 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 311 animation: none; 312 } 313 ``` 314 315 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 316 317 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 318 319 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 320 321 #### Respecting reduced motion 322 323 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. Morphs, reveals, and crossfades carry less risk since they affect smaller areas or rely on opacity rather than position. 324 325 The simplest approach is to disable all animation durations: 326 327 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 328 @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { 329 ::view-transition-old(*), 330 ::view-transition-new(*), 331 ::view-transition-group(*) { 332 animation-duration: 0s !important; 333 animation-delay: 0s !important; 334 } 335 } 336 ``` 337 338 Without animation, content swaps instantly, which is the browser's default behavior. A more refined approach would preserve crossfades and opacity transitions while removing positional movement. See ["No Motion Isn't Always prefers-reduced-motion"](https://css-tricks.com/nuking-motion-with-prefers-reduced-motion/) for more on this. 339 340 ### Step 4: Crossfade content within the same route 341 342 The gallery has a photographer section with tabs. Each tab shows a different photographer's photos, but the route structure is the same: `/collection/[slug]`. Clicking between tabs does not feel like navigating to a new page. It feels like switching content within the same container. 343 344 A directional slide would be wrong here. Slides communicate "going to a new place." A crossfade communicates "same place, different content." The container persists (continuity), only the grid inside changes (swap). 345 346 Use a `ViewTransition` with `key` set to the current slug. When the key changes, React triggers a transition between the old and new content: 347 348 ```tsx filename="app/collection/[slug]/page.tsx" 349 import { Suspense, ViewTransition } from 'react' 350 351 export default async function CollectionPage({ params }) { 352 const { slug } = await params 353 354 return ( 355 }> 356 363 364 365 366 ) 367 } 368 ``` 369 370 The `share="auto"` and `enter="auto"` props tell React to use its default crossfade animation. The `name` prop gives the container an identity so React knows what to animate. The `key={slug}` change is what triggers the transition. 371 372 If we click between photographer tabs, the grid crossfades. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Only the photo grid transitions between states. 373 374 ## Next steps 375 376 You now know how to use view transitions to communicate meaning during navigation. Shared elements communicate continuity across routes. Suspense reveals animate loading handoffs. Directional slides encode navigation history. Crossfades signal content changes within the same location. 377 378 Each pattern answers a different question for the user: 379 380 | Pattern | What it communicates | 381 | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | 382 | Shared element (morph) | "Same thing, going deeper" | 383 | Suspense reveal | "Data loaded" | 384 | Directional slide | "Going forward / coming back" | 385 | Same-route crossfade | "Same place, different content" | 386 387 For API details and more patterns: 388 389 - [View transition configuration](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/viewTransition) 390 - [Link `transitionTypes` prop](/docs/app/api-reference/components/link#transitiontypes) 391 - [`useRouter`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router) — also supports `transitionTypes` in `push()` and `replace()` 392 - [React `ViewTransition` component](https://react.dev/reference/react/ViewTransition) 393 - [Complete CSS from this guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/react-view-transitions-demo/blob/main/src/app/globals.css) — all keyframes and view transition rules in one file 394

Build succeeds. Here's what was implemented:

**1. Shared element morphing** — Both the grid thumbnail (`ProductGrid.tsx`) and the detail hero (`product/[slug]/page.tsx`) are wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`}>` with matching names. The browser automatically morphs the image between its grid position and the hero slot.

**2. Directional navigation slides** — Grid links use `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}` and the back link uses `transitionTypes={['nav-back']}`. Both pages wrap their content in a `<ViewTransition>` that maps these types to directional slide animations (content slides left on forward, right on back).

**3. Suspense reveal animations** — Skeleton fallbacks are wrapped with `<ViewTransition exit="slide-down">` and resolved content with `<ViewTransition enter="slide-up" default="none">`. The skeleton slides down/fades out, then content slides up/fades in with asymmetric timing (150ms exit, 210ms enter).

**4. Reduced motion** — A `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` rule zeros out all animation durations and delays on all view transition pseudo-elements, making transitions instant for users who prefer reduced motion.

**Config** — `experimental.viewTransition: true` enabled in `next.config.ts`.
